Narrator: IELTS listening, version 54562. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts.

Narrator: Write all your answers in the listening question booklet. At the end of the test, you will be given 10 minutes to transfer your answers to an answer sheet. Now turn to Part One, on page two of your question booklet. Part One.

Narrator: You will hear a conversation between a father and the person he is employed to look after his young daughter, who is called Lily, during the school holidays. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.

Father: Okay, Claire, let's sit down and plan some activities for you and Lily to enjoy together over the school holidays while I'm at work.

Claire: All right, I'll get a pen and paper.

Father: Please feel free to make suggestions of your own. But I thought a nice way to start the holidays would be to take Lily to a film on Monday.

Claire: Nice idea.

Father: I've got two 10-pound film vouchers I can give you.

Claire: Oh, Mr Scott, you can't use those during the holidays. Why don't I go on the internet and pre-book the tickets? They're usually nine pounds 75, but this month they're only eight pounds 25 if you get them through the website.

Father: Great idea. Now, Lily usually likes to have a drink during the film, but I'd prefer that she didn't have juice or anything with sugar in.

Claire: Yes, that would be bad for her teeth. So, how about some water?

Father: Good idea. You can buy that at the cinema.

Claire: Okay. How about Tuesday? Maybe we could do something outdoors.

Father: Well, I did see an advertisement in the local paper for families to get together for a walk. It looks like it could be fun.

Claire: That would be perfect. It'll be nice to meet up with some other children as well. I suppose that's in the park.

Father: Let me check. No, you need to meet in the woods. You know where that is, don't you? Not far from the river. And I'd better check the time for you. Oh yes, here it is. The walk actually starts at 10.15 in the morning, but I think you'd better be there at 10 to give you time to find the other families.

Claire: That's fine. I'll make sure I leave the house by 9.30, so I have time to get there. Shall I take Lily's pushchair? Do you think?

Father: No, I don't think you'll need it. But you'd better take her boots in case it's muddy. You'll find them in the cupboard in the hallway.

Narrator: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to 10. Now listen and answer questions seven to 10.

Father: Now on Wednesday, Lily's been invited to a party that's being held for her cousin.

Claire: Lovely.

Father: Yes, it's a shame I'll have to miss it. Now the party was going to be in their garden, but they've decided to have it in a restaurant now instead. They've chosen the one in the high street. They have staff who dress up and put on a show for the children, so they. Should enjoy it.

Claire: Great. Now I see on your calendar, Mr Scott, that Lily has a music lesson every Thursday. Does this continue over the holidays?

Father: Oh yes, I'd forgotten about that.

Claire: It says school on the calendar. Is that where I should take her?

Father: It was there, but not during the holidays. This week it's at Akehurst Hall. It's right at the top of the hill. You can't miss it.

Claire: Oh, actually, I think I know the place.

Father: Great. And remember, you need to pay for that. I'll put the money in an envelope for you.

Claire: Okay. I'll make a note of that in my diary.

Father: You're very organized. I like that.

Claire: Thanks. Now I've had an idea about Friday. If you haven't got anything planned already,

Father: yes.

Claire: A friend of mine told me about a storytelling event. It's on at the bookshop. Would Lily like to go?

Father: Oh yes, we've been there before, actually. She loved it. Oh, I've just remembered the laundry will be ready by then. Can you pick that up afterwards? And next door to the cleaners is the post office. Could you please get me some stamps? I need to send some letters and a postcard, so that would be very helpful.

Claire: Sure. Now, can I ask you a few questions?

Narrator: That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.

Narrator: You will hear a podcast about volunteering to work for a charity called The Hub, which provides reading support for blind people. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16

Janice: I'm Janice Clark, and I'm the manager of the charity called The Hub, which provides a wide range of volunteer services for blind people, such as providing recordings of books and magazines, the Hub Charity is based in a small village called Ivy Brook, which it's called home since 1990.

Janice: We now have nearly 75 volunteers working for us in some capacity, but when it was first set up in 1980, there were only 25. All of them were doing recorded readings for the blind. Nowadays, we offer a great deal more, which means we need a wide range of volunteers with different expertise, as I'll explain in a few moments.

Janice: The Hub is entirely dependent on donations. We have very generous gifts from local businesses, though the most significant contribution has always come from individual supporters, we also get an increasing amount from school groups who arrange various benefit events to make money for us.

Janice: Some people hear about us because a friend or relative with sight problems already makes use of our services and tells them about how valuable the Hub is, or they may hear about us from someone they meet who is already a volunteer. That's how most people join us, in fact.

Janice: But our website also attracted quite a lot of interest from people who want to support us.

Janice: There are certain areas of the operation, where we particularly need volunteers at the moment, this week, one group are involved in addressing envelopes containing recordings in digital form, which have been requested by almost 10,000 users all over the country.

Janice: But what we're specifically looking for at this time are people to help make sure our lists of recordings and other materials are accurate, so we don't waste time on unnecessary repeats. I feel strongly that we're a friendly and open organization, and we listen carefully to any comments about negative aspects of working at the Hub.

Janice: Ivy Brook is an interesting location. It's very close to the countryside, but there are some local shops to nip out to and buy stuff for lunch or a snack. There's plenty of space. In our old town center location, we had lots of problems with parking, but not here.

Janice: However, the volunteers tell us the rooms can feel rather cold in the winter, so we're investing in a new boiler. Until it's installed, you'd better wrap up. We're also a dynamic organization, always on the lookout to provide services our users really need.

Janice: Responding to requests, we started a service where volunteers visit blind people in their homes. We also set up a reading group where every month a different book is discussed. Holding events at the Hub has been very successful, and I hope to organize music lessons there in the near future as well.

Janice: We have lots of soundproof studios available for them. We're organizing fundraising for that at the moment.

Narrator: Before you hear the rest of the podcast, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20.

Janice: And what types of reading requests are growing most quickly? Of course, novels are always popular, as you can imagine, as are local newspapers. But we're seeing a rapid increase in numbers asking for magazines.

Janice: Children's stories are not often asked for, but we're now doing a lot of work for schools, with a big increase in requests for textbooks, which require tremendous concentration by our volunteer readers because they have to get them absolutely correct.

Janice: We have a group of dedicated readers who are extremely skilled, but even they find certain types of text difficult to read aloud. Of course, it's sensible to ask people to read what interests them personally. There's quite a lot of demand for technical stuff.

Janice: We give cricket reports to sports enthusiasts, and chess players find the details of game summaries pretty easy. But however keen you are at crafts, knitting instructions are always a real challenge for everyone, and motoring magazines have pages and pages of detailed descriptions, which even car lovers hate reading.

Janice: So, if anyone out there is interested.

Narrator: Part three. You will hear two final year tourism students called Hannah and Martin discussing parts of the career planning module they have just completed. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.

Hannah: Martin, we need to discuss our feedback for Dr. Mason.

Martin: Yes, about the career planning module.

Hannah: Right. Let's start with the part on opportunities in tourism.

Martin: Good. The first session was the seminar with two recruitment specialists. Did you go to that?

Hannah: Yes, they had all those visuals which helped fix the points they made in your mind. So, all the details about contracts and things weren't as boring as they might have been.

Martin: Yes, it'd be hard to forget that session.

Hannah: What about the presentations given by employers?

Martin: It was great to get clear and relevant tips, which we can use straight away in our job applications.

Hannah: Exactly.

Martin: Now, what about the networking event when we met all those people from the tourism industry-that really made me think about how my career might develop in the long term, and what sort of choices I might have to make.

Hannah: That's interesting, 'cause I felt the same. I'd been wondering whether to go into catering or travel eventually. Finally, we had the interview with the hotel manager. That could have been planned better, as we didn't have enough time with her. But personally, I was more sure of myself after that and ready to take the next step.

Martin: Yes, I felt very positive afterwards. So, what's next?

Narrator: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30.

Hannah: We need to review the rest of the careers’ advice module. Let's talk about the online assessment we did. I thought it would check what we knew about our subject, which I was a bit worried about, but actually it was to indicate what sort of job would be best for each of us?

Martin: I wasn't keen to do it, but it was useful. What about the visit from the career coach? I didn't get much information there.

Hannah: I enjoyed that personally. She wasn't the most engaging speaker, but I liked the way that we all had to get involved and take part in the discussion.

Martin: Absolutely, that was a good way of doing it. I just found some later speakers more informative.

Hannah: Um, then there was the activity day we spent off campus at the exhibition center. That was fun, wasn't it?

Martin: And practical, as it felt as though the activities and exercises were exactly the sort of thing we might be doing in future jobs.

Hannah: Definitely, and personally, I enjoyed being given time limits and having to work quickly, but I just like that kind of thing.

Martin: I don't, but the training was expertly done, and the staff had plenty of knowledge to share.

Hannah: I thought the practice job interviews were useful.

Martin: Did you? I spent ages preparing my letter of application, and I can't say I found that to be a good use of time.

Hannah: Nor me, but it was good to learn about ways of talking about our experience and supporting the claims we make about the skills we have.

Martin: Yes, that was good, but they did go on about the importance of the handshake and how you sit and so on, and we'd already talked about that hundreds of times.

Hannah: The feedback I got from my tutor on this module was really useful. She told me that I didn't participate enough when we were talking in groups, so I forced myself to join in. And actually, I quite enjoyed it. I've always got lots of ideas from books and articles, but before that, I found it easier to express my ideas in writing.

Martin: Right. Finally, there's the survey we did with other students on the course.

Hannah: Let's just look at the results of that.

Martin: Did anyone mention how the assessments were graded? I felt sometimes different teachers valued different things.

Hannah: Well, that didn't come up from other students. A few said they hadn't clearly understood the aims of the course. Should we raise that in our feedback?

Martin: Looking at their comments, though, that was because they didn't do their research properly at the start.

Hannah: Okay.

Martin: A more significant point raised is the titles and guidelines for assignments. Students said they often got the wrong idea and needed tutors' help to make tasks clear.

Hannah: Right, that's something we need to bring up then. Anything else?

Martin: I think that's it. Now we need to start writing things up.

Narrator: That is the end of part three. You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part.

Narrator: Part four. You will hear a university lecture by a guest speaker who works at the Environmental Protection Agency in Australia. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

Mark James: My name's Mark James, and I'm an officer with the Environmental Protection Agency, our job is to examine building proposals sent to the government by construction companies to determine their risk to the environment. We do this in the form of an environmental report, which I'll now outline for you today.

Mark James: Firstly, the company sends us their project description, outlining each part of their proposal. In the next stage, we produce an area description. We need to formally catalog the wildlife within the project's proposed perimeter and determine whether any species will be threatened by the development.

Mark James: Next is the mitigation stage, where we use the information from stage two to make recommendations for how the company can avoid any negative environmental impact. With the construction of wind turbines, for example, we might recommend avoiding the months when birds are nesting.

Mark James: Next, we produce the non-technical summary, which looks at the operation's objectives and its potential impact on the area in question. We make sure the information doesn't contain any jargon that will interfere with the message, and that it's written in simple language. We then issue this to the public, and invite feedback.

Mark James: And finally, we prepare the final report, communicating our proposed action to the construction company. Let's look at one particular construction proposal that we worked on recently for a project on Barrow Island. Barrow Island is around 70 kilometers off the western Australian coast.

Mark James: It's unique because thousands of years ago it was separated from the mainland. The flora and fauna of the island are different because they've been able to grow unaffected by the events and factors that have, over time, influenced the natural environment of the mainland.

Mark James: By this, I mean the introduction of non-native animals like foxes and cats. The island has also been spared the environmental impact of farming. I should say at the outset that industry has already existed on the island for several decades.

Mark James: The first was in the 1930s when fishing was established here on a commercial basis, about 10 men would inhabit the island for six months of the year and operate within a 20-kilometer radius during the annual season. Then, in the 1950s, mining was established, employing around 150 people.

Mark James: The existing industry I've just described is a completely different issue to the construction project proposed by Chandler Developers, though. Chandler Developers wanted to construct a plant on Barrow Island that would allow them to extract gas from way out in the deep waters off the coast of Australia.

Mark James: They would then clean it up and compress it into a liquid, and then sell it to a range of places like China and Japan and so forth. Construction was to occur over three years, employing around 6000 people, bringing in millions of tons of equipment and materials.

Mark James: Now, of course, with this kind of major invasion, the government was deeply concerned about the environmental impact. Barrow Island's two main beaches, which are home to a variety of marine life, are located on either side of the proposed development.

Mark James: The amount of noise generated by this project would cause extreme anxiety to the local turtle population in particular, as they use these beaches for breeding and laying eggs, we were also concerned that any baby turtles that hatch and do manage to find the water could become disorientated and totally at the mercy of predators.

Mark James: Fortunately, saltwater crocodiles are not found in this area, but sharks are common and represent the main risk to the local marine life, and particularly the defenseless baby turtles.

Mark James: Another issue we had is with the sheer size of the project, which would require large numbers of people to come onto the island during the construction period. This would create a very real danger of pests being brought with them.

Mark James: It would be catastrophic for the wildlife, and indeed the entire ecology of the island, if, for example, a population of rats were to become established. So, there were very real issues with this project, and our report recommended that it not proceed.

Narrator: That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
